stem: A 67-year-old develops sudden severe left eye pain, haloes around lights, vomiting and headache. The eye is red with a mid-dilated poorly reactive pupil, cloudy cornea and markedly raised intraocular pressure. Vision is blurred.
ask: What is the BEST immediate management?
options: Treat with topical lubricants and routine optometry follow-up.
Patch both eyes for 48 hours to reduce exposure to bright light.
Start pressure-lowering medications promptly and arrange same-day ophthalmology for definitive laser iridotomy planning.
Give oral antihistamine for presumed allergic conjunctivitis.
Give cyclopentolate to dilate the pupil for examination before consulting ophthalmology.
explanations: This is a vision-threatening pressure emergency, not simple dry eye.
Occlusive patching does not lower intraocular pressure and delays care.
Correct: urgent pressure reduction protects vision while specialist treatment addresses the pupillary block.
Allergic conjunctivitis causes itching and watery discharge, not a fixed pupil and severe ocular pressure.
Dilating the pupil can exacerbate angle closure.
pearl: Painful red eye with mid-dilated pupil, corneal haze and systemic nausea is acute angle closure until proven otherwise.
pivot: Painless gradual visual blurring with a normal pupil suggests a different process such as cataract.

steps: Recognise and refer
Check visual acuity, pupil and IOP if safe; immediate ophthalmology referral.
Lower IOP
Topical aqueous suppressants and systemic acetazolamide when appropriate; consider hyperosmotic agent if severe by specialist advice.
Treat cause
Laser peripheral iridotomy once pressure/cornea permits, including fellow-eye risk assessment.
Follow
Monitor vision, pressure and contraindications to glaucoma drops.
management.safety: Avoid mydriatic medications and delay for routine outpatient review.
management.local: Practical teaching aid, not a treatment order; confirm local surgical, specialty and prescribing protocols.

skill: Central retinal artery occlusion / stroke link
stem: A 71-year-old with AF awakens with sudden painless complete loss of vision in one eye two hours ago. The eye is white; fundus reveals a pale retina and cherry-red spot. No eye pain or trauma is reported.
options: Give steroid eye drops and review in one week.
Treat as a stroke equivalent: activate urgent retinal/neurological pathway and assess embolic and reperfusion options.
Arrange routine cataract surgery consultation.
Give empirical antiviral drops for herpes keratitis.
Reassure because vision usually returns fully without intervention.
explanations: This is acute retinal ischaemia requiring emergency neurovascular assessment, not inflammation.
Correct: acute CRAO is retinal infarction with time-dependent treatment consideration and systemic stroke risk.
Cataract causes gradual opacity, not sudden profound monocular loss.
Keratitis causes pain, photophobia and corneal findings, not a cherry-red retinal spot.
CRAO may cause permanent visual loss and signals elevated future stroke risk.
pearl: Sudden painless monocular blindness is a vascular emergency until excluded; consider amaurosis fugax and giant-cell arteritis based on clues.
pivot: If associated temporal headache, jaw claudication or systemic inflammation, start a giant-cell arteritis pathway immediately.

steps: Activate
Emergency ophthalmology and stroke service evaluation; exact onset and visual acuity.
Assess stroke risk
ECG/AF, carotid/cardiac source, neuroimaging and vascular studies as appropriate.
Discuss acute treatment
Eligibility for time-window reperfusion strategies and other specialist approaches under current local pathways.
Prevent recurrence
Antithrombotic and vascular risk management after mechanism assessment.
management.safety: Do not delay referral to try unproven ocular massage as sole care.
management.local: Practical teaching aid, not a treatment order; confirm local surgical, specialty and prescribing protocols.

skill: Giant cell arteritis and vision preservation
stem: A 76-year-old develops new temporal headache, scalp tenderness, jaw pain when chewing and transient dimming of vision in the left eye. ESR is 95 mm/h, CRP elevated, and the temporal artery feels thickened.
ask: What is the BEST immediate treatment?
options: Await temporal artery biopsy before giving treatment.
Give only aspirin and arrange an outpatient CT head.
Start oral antibiotics for presumed temporal-artery infection.
Give high-dose glucocorticoids immediately and arrange urgent ophthalmology/rheumatology assessment and confirmatory testing.
Prescribe migraine prophylaxis and review after six weeks.
explanations: Biopsy confirmation is important but delaying steroids risks irreversible bilateral blindness.
Antiplatelet therapy does not replace urgent glucocorticoids for threatened GCA vision.
GCA is immune-mediated large-vessel vasculitis, not routine bacterial arteritis.
Correct: cranial GCA with visual symptoms needs immediate steroid therapy before biopsy/imaging.
New headache with jaw claudication, raised inflammatory markers and visual symptoms is a major ischaemic warning.
pearl: Suspected cranial giant cell arteritis with visual symptoms is a treat-before-confirmation emergency.
pivot: Polymyalgia rheumatica without cranial ischaemia often uses lower-dose steroid regimens and a different urgency.

steps: Recognise
Assess monocular vision change, jaw claudication, scalp symptoms and large-vessel signs; FBC/ESR/CRP.
Treat now
Immediate high-dose corticosteroid, often IV for threatened visual loss per specialist protocol.
Confirm
Urgent temporal-artery ultrasound/biopsy without stopping treatment; consider vascular imaging.
Protect
Monitor glucose, BP, bone risk and assess fellow eye.
management.safety: Avoid waiting for biopsy or normalisation of inflammatory markers before treatment.
management.local: Practical teaching aid, not a treatment order; confirm local surgical, specialty and prescribing protocols.

stem: A 21-year-old has four days of unilateral severe sore throat, fever, muffled 'hot potato' voice and difficulty opening his mouth. Uvula deviates away from a bulging tonsillar pillar; he can handle secretions and oxygenation is normal.
options: Urgent ENT review for drainage plus antibiotics and analgesia after airway assessment.
Give routine antiviral medication only and discharge.
Use inhaled salbutamol as first-line to treat the altered voice.
Perform elective tonsillectomy without assessing infection or hydration.
Treat solely with oral antihistamine for presumed allergic oedema.
explanations: Correct: classic peritonsillar abscess requires drainage assessment and antimicrobial coverage.
The unilateral fluctuant tonsillar swelling and uvular deviation point to bacterial abscess rather than HSV.
Upper oropharyngeal pathology does not respond to bronchodilator.
Acute abscess care is immediate assessment, antibiotics, drainage; surgery is selective.
Fever, trismus and uvular deviation are not typical allergy.
pearl: Trismus, unilateral tonsillar swelling and uvular deviation distinguish peritonsillar abscess from uncomplicated pharyngitis.
pivot: Drooling, stridor, tripod posture or inability to handle secretions suggests dangerous airway infection and changes priorities.

steps: Airway first
Check voice, stridor, drooling and ability to swallow; summon senior airway help if threatened.
Treat infection
Analgesia, hydration, appropriate oral/IV antibiotics and ENT assessment.
Drain
Needle aspiration or incision and drainage where indicated by trained clinician.
Reassess
Ensure oral intake, improvement and return precautions; consider recurrent tonsillitis history.
management.safety: Never attempt forceful examination or drainage with an unsecured airway.
management.local: Practical teaching aid, not a treatment order; confirm local surgical, specialty and prescribing protocols.

stem: A 48-year-old notices a sudden severe hearing loss in the right ear on waking 18 hours ago. Otoscopy is normal, Rinne is positive bilaterally and Weber lateralises to the left. No vertigo or focal neurological deficit is reported.
ask: What is the BEST next management?
options: Wait one month because sudden unilateral loss is usually wax.
Arrange same-day ENT/audiology assessment with prompt corticosteroid treatment consideration.
Start antibiotic ear drops for presumed otitis externa.
Arrange elective grommet insertion.
Recommend hearing aids only without investigating the onset.
explanations: Normal otoscopy and tuning forks indicate sensorineural loss, not impacted cerumen.
Correct: sudden sensorineural hearing loss is a time-sensitive otological emergency.
No ear canal inflammation or conductive findings support otitis externa.
Middle-ear ventilation tubes treat selected conductive conditions, not sudden inner-ear loss.
Rehabilitation may follow, but acute potentially salvageable hearing loss needs urgent assessment.
pearl: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss warrants urgent referral, ideally within 24 hours, because early treatment improves recovery chances.
pivot: Unilateral hearing loss with pain/effusion and a negative Rinne suggests conductive disease needing a different pathway.

steps: Identify type
History and examination, otoscopy, tuning forks, neurologic screen and audiogram.
Refer urgently
ENT assessment for oral or intratympanic steroids based on contraindications/time window.
Investigate
Consider MRI internal auditory canals to exclude retrocochlear cause after urgent treatment planning.
Follow
Repeat audiometry and hearing rehabilitation if deficit persists.
management.safety: Stroke symptoms, vertigo with neurological signs or facial weakness require emergency neurological assessment.
management.local: Practical teaching aid, not a treatment order; confirm local surgical, specialty and prescribing protocols.

stem: A 34-year-old after a fall has a deformed forearm with a 4 cm wound communicating with visible bone. Distal pulse and sensation are present, BP stable. There is gravel contamination.
ask: Which treatment sequence is MOST appropriate?
options: Close the skin tightly in ED then review in one week.
Give oral antibiotics only and splint without surgery.
Irrigate in the ward until the wound looks clean, then omit antibiotics.
Give timely IV antibiotics/tetanus prophylaxis, cover and splint the limb and arrange urgent operative debridement.
Delay all intervention until formal CT angiography despite intact neurovascular examination.
explanations: Primary closure before formal irrigation/debridement can trap contamination.
Open fractures usually need IV antibiotics, tetanus assessment and operative debridement/fixation.
Visual cleanliness does not exclude contamination; early systemic antibiotics matter.
Correct: infection prevention begins immediately, with definitive surgery guided by fracture and wound severity.
Imaging may be helpful selectively but cannot delay antibiotics and wound care.
pearl: Open fractures require early IV antibiotics, sterile coverage, neurovascular documentation and surgical source control.
pivot: A closed fracture without skin communication has different infection prophylaxis and operative urgency.

steps: Document neurovascular state
Before/after splint, assess pulses, perfusion, motor and sensation; photograph according to consent/policy.
Protect
Remove gross debris only when appropriate, saline-moistened sterile cover, immobilise and treat pain.
Prevent infection
Prompt IV antibiotics selected for grade and contamination, tetanus assessment.
Operate
Urgent orthopaedic/plastic assessment for debridement and stabilisation.
management.safety: Do not repeatedly probe the open wound or perform unplanned closure.
management.local: Practical teaching aid, not a treatment order; confirm local surgical, specialty and prescribing protocols.

stem: A 70-year-old with a knee replacement three months ago has rapidly increasing joint pain, swelling and temperature 38.4°C. CRP is 172 mg/L; ultrasound shows an effusion and radiograph reveals no fracture. He remains haemodynamically stable.
ask: Which is the BEST next step?
options: Urgent orthopaedic assessment and sterile joint aspiration with blood cultures before targeted treatment where safe.
Start intra-articular corticosteroid for presumed postoperative synovitis.
Arrange routine annual review as swelling is common after replacement.
Remove the prosthesis in ED without cultures or specialist planning.
Give a one-day oral antibiotic course without further assessment.
explanations: Correct: suspected prosthetic joint infection needs microbiological diagnosis and coordinated surgical/antibiotic strategy.
Steroid injection risks worsening infection.
Fever, effusion and high inflammation require urgent evaluation.
Prosthetic source control requires orthopaedic expertise and surgery planning.
Short therapy may sterilise cultures and inadequately treat biofilm infection.
pearl: Prosthetic joint infection differs from native septic arthritis because biofilm and implant retention/exchange strategies matter.
pivot: If haemodynamically unstable/septic, start broad IV antibiotics promptly after feasible cultures without waiting for aspiration.

steps: Recognise
Assess fever, wound/drainage and joint function; urgent orthopaedic/infection referral.
Sample
Blood cultures and aseptic joint aspiration for cell count, cultures and crystals when stable.
Treat
Specialist-directed IV antibiotics and debridement/implant-retention or revision strategy by onset/stability.
Follow
Monitor inflammatory response and prolonged organism-specific therapy.
management.safety: Avoid starting antibiotics before necessary cultures when stable, but never delay in shock.
management.local: Practical teaching aid, not a treatment order; confirm local surgical, specialty and prescribing protocols.

stem: A 17-year-old has sudden severe left testicular pain for four hours, vomiting, a high-riding horizontal testis and absent cremasteric reflex. No dysuria, fever or trauma. Surgical help is immediately available.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate action?
options: Arrange routine ultrasound tomorrow before deciding on surgery.
Give oral antibiotics for epididymitis and follow up in a week.
Urgent urological exploration and detorsion/orchiopexy without imaging delay.
Advise bed rest until pain resolves spontaneously.
Perform scrotal needle aspiration for suspected abscess.
explanations: Time-sensitive torsion should not wait when clinical suspicion is high and exploration is available.
Classic sudden pain, high position and absent reflex indicate torsion, not infection.
Correct: salvage falls with time, and contralateral fixation is usually performed.
Spontaneous partial detorsion may occur but risks recurrence/necrosis and is not safe management.
No features support abscess and invasive aspiration would delay surgery.
pearl: Testicular torsion is a clinical time emergency; prompt surgical exploration outranks Doppler when suspicion is high.
pivot: Gradual scrotal pain with urinary symptoms and preserved cremasteric reflex may suggest epididymitis, though torsion must still be excluded.

steps: Recognise
Assess time since onset, lie/reflexes and abdominal/groin findings; NPO and analgesia.
Mobilise surgery
Urgent urology/theatre, do not delay for Doppler if high suspicion.
Definitive
Surgical detorsion and bilateral orchiopexy when viable; orchidectomy if nonviable.
Counsel
Fertility risk and prompt return for contralateral or recurrent pain.
management.safety: Manual detorsion by trained staff may buy time but must not replace operative exploration.
management.local: Practical teaching aid, not a treatment order; confirm local surgical, specialty and prescribing protocols.

stem: A 69-year-old with AF develops sudden left leg pain and coldness. Left foot is pale, no Doppler arterial signals are heard, and she has new paraesthesia but can still move her toes. Onset was two hours ago.
ask: Which immediate management is MOST appropriate?
options: Give intravenous unfractionated heparin after contraindication assessment and urgently involve vascular surgery for revascularisation.
Schedule elective exercise ABI testing in three months.
Prescribe aspirin alone and discharge if pain improves.
Compress the limb and elevate it above heart level to improve venous drainage.
Delay all therapy until angiography results are reported tomorrow.
explanations: Correct: acute limb ischaemia needs rapid anticoagulation and definitive reperfusion planning.
A pulseless cold leg with sensory changes is a vascular emergency.
Antiplatelet alone is inadequate for an acutely threatened limb.
Compression/elevation may worsen arterial perfusion.
Anticoagulation and vascular assessment should not wait for routine imaging in a threatened limb.
pearl: The 6 Ps (pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, paralysis, poikilothermia) help recognise acute limb ischaemia.
pivot: Chronic claudication without acute rest pain or neurologic deficit follows outpatient vascular risk management.

steps: Recognise
Check motor/sensory function, arterial Doppler, other limb and embolic source; activate vascular team.
Anticoagulate
IV unfractionated heparin if safe; give analgesia and protect foot.
Image/reperfuse
CTA or operative angiography according to limb viability and urgency; thrombectomy/thrombolysis/surgery as indicated.
Reassess
Monitor reperfusion injury, compartment syndrome, renal function and potassium.
management.safety: New paralysis or fixed mottling indicates a more severely threatened or irreversible limb.
management.local: Practical teaching aid, not a treatment order; confirm local surgical, specialty and prescribing protocols.

skill: Bowel obstruction / internal hernia after bariatric surgery
stem: A 41-year-old four years after Roux-en-Y bypass has recurrent severe colicky abdominal pain and vomiting. CT shows mesenteric swirl and dilated proximal bowel; lactate is initially normal. She remains stable but in considerable pain.
ask: Which next action is MOST appropriate?
options: Discharge because a normal lactate excludes bowel ischaemia.
Give osmotic laxatives until the stool output improves.
Repeat CT in six months because chronic post-bypass pain is common.
Start empirical antibiotics only and avoid surgical review.
Arrange prompt bariatric/general surgical evaluation with low threshold for diagnostic laparoscopy.
explanations: Lactate may remain normal early; internal hernia can strangulate bowel rapidly.
Mechanical obstruction due to internal hernia is not relieved by laxatives.
Mesenteric swirl with obstruction requires urgent surgical assessment.
Source control is needed if internal hernia threatens intestinal blood supply.
Correct: internal hernia after bypass may cause closed-loop obstruction and bowel loss despite normal early labs.
pearl: Post–Roux-en-Y intermittent severe pain with mesenteric swirl should trigger concern for internal hernia.
pivot: Uncomplicated marginal ulcer after bypass usually causes epigastric pain without obstructed loops/mesenteric swirl.

steps: Assess
NPO, IV fluids, analgesia, electrolytes and serial exam.
Escalate
Immediate bariatric or general surgeon discussion and review of operative anatomy/CT.
Operate where needed
Urgent diagnostic laparoscopy and reduction/defect closure if suspected strangulation.
Watch
Repeat vitals, pain, lactate and perfusion, but do not rely on normal values to exclude ischaemia.
management.safety: Delayed diagnosis can lead to extensive small-bowel infarction.
management.local: Practical teaching aid, not a treatment order; confirm local surgical, specialty and prescribing protocols.
